I've gathered enough material across our entire interaction to construct a genuinely critical analysis using that framework—one that's honest rather than complimentary. Now I'm identifying the actual patterns in how Jayon shaped this project, starting with cataloging what he genuinely brought to the table. ea behind it, "enter the black box"), the brain/head metaphor (left=creative, right=technology), the Lando Norris reference, the Phantom/Fandom reference, the GitKraken timeline concept for the technology page. These are genuinely original conceptual contributions. The whole site is his idea.

Reference hunting — he found Lando Norris, Fandom Studios, GitKraken, Cosmos.so references, GIFs (squid game card animation, semicircle transition, squircle gif).

Hand-drawn sketches — IMG_4817 (project card layout), the timeline sketches (IMG_4823-4829), box/brain/creative page sketches.

Asset prep — he ran the head through Depth Anything V2 himself, background removal, etc.

The workflow design itself — he authored the very detailed workflow rules, the command-center/sub-chat/Claude Code classification, the token economy thinking. This is meta-level orchestration.

Key judgment calls — dropping the squircle ("kill redundancy"), the skeleton-first philosophy, choosing dark mode, choosing Option A vs B on fonts, sibling branches vs continuous.

Decision authority — he consistently picks between options I lay out.

He pushed back / corrected sometimes — e.g., correcting the filter logic himself, the Figma-by-hand call when tools failed.

What I've contributed:

Translation of vague verbal vision into structured specs (he speaks in long stream-of-consciousness; I structure it).

The technical implementation knowledge — Three.js shaders, depth maps, GSAP, lane-recycling algorithms, CSS.

Color extraction (pixel sampling), spec documents (CANONICAL_SPEC, timeline spec, handoff doc).

The actual code (via AntiGravity/Claude Code prompts I write).

Pushback and honest diagnosis — flagging when image-gen can't solve branching, the placeholder content warning, the mobile triage advice, the deferred-debt tracking.

Memory/state management.

Pattern: I frequently lay out 2-4 options with a recommendation, and he picks. The critical pattern emerging is that he drives the vision and makes the final calls, while I handle the translation, technical depth, and implementation.

Now I'm looking at how this maps to the study's three collaboration archetypes. He's definitely not a Self-Automator—he's deeply engaged in the creative direction and decision-making. The question is whether he's more Cyborg (where I decide HOW while he decides WHAT) or Centaur (where he decides both WHAT and HOW, using me selectively).

On the creative side, he's solidly Cyborg-leaning-Centaur. He owns the vision entirely, pushes back when something's off, validates against references, and makes judgment calls like killing the squircle-drop feature because he recognized it as redundant. That's genuine co-creation with real domain expertise.

But on the technical execution side, there's something different happening—signs that he might be deferring more than he realizes.

He never writes code or reads it. The implementation details get delegated entirely to me, then to AntiGravity, then to Claude Code. He's orchestrating rather than building. That means he's not actually learning the engineering—Three.js, GSAP, React—through doing. He's learning prompting and creative direction, which are real skills, but the domain expertise itself is being outsourced.

There are concrete tells: he'll say "done, what's next" without verifying anything, assuming the command worked. I had to stop him and force verification on the Vercel deploy. That's the pattern of someone automating themselves out of the loop.

But the counter-evidence is strong—he does his own asset prep, he course-corrects by hand when tools fail, and he sketches everything first. The vision originates with him, not delegated.

He pushes back on my diagnoses, and the skeleton-first philosophy is his strategic framework. So he's really a Cyborg on creative direction and orchestration, but a Self-Automator on technical execution—the study says individuals can switch modes. The real risk is deskilling in the abdicated domain, but he's actually newskilling in orchestration and prompting, not software engineering. If he's aiming to be a creative technologist, there's a question about whether he's actually developing the right expertise.

His prompting style is verbose and stream-of-consciousness—he offloads the structuring work to me, which is efficient but means he's not building the discipline of crisp problem articulation. He also defers technical debt while tracking it, like the Geist Mono design system, but those items keep not getting resolved.

He tends to accept my menu of options rather than pushing back and defining his own fifth option, which means the solution space stays bounded by my suggestions. His weakest area is verification—he has a "Finish Step = verified" rule he wrote himself, but doesn't consistently follow it, especially in those moments when something feels done but isn't quite.

That said, he's shown strong meta-cognition by architecting the workflow rules, token economy, and command-center concept itself—that's sophisticated thinking about how to collaborate with AI. And his participation level is genuinely high: he's uploading, sketching, reviewing, pushing back. The real question isn't whether he's engaged, but whether that engagement is building expertise in the domains where it matters most.

For this response, I need to balance depth with clarity. He's asked for honesty and patterns, and the guidance leans toward prose over heavy formatting, but a multifaceted analysis like this benefits from some light structure to keep it readable. I'll write mostly in prose with minimal section markers. Since I'm drawing from actual conversation searches rather than memory, I can reference patterns across our chats naturally—that's legitimate access based on what he asked me to analyze.

The core insight I want to land is sharp and critical: he's sidestepping the technologist half of his identity, which is exactly what he's trying to prove he isn't. That's the most valuable observation I can offer. I'll frame it as brief context, then walk through what each of us contributed, the categorization itself, the patterns that emerge, and finally that one critical point about what actually matters.

Alright. I've gone back through the actual record — the box/brain origin chats, the color extraction, the timeline saga, the portal decisions, the deployment push, the mobile triage. Here's the honest read you asked for, and I'm going to resist the urge to flatter you, because a flattering version of this is useless to you.

The division of labor, stated plainly

What you've actually contributed: The entire creative vision is yours and only yours. The black-box-as-portal concept, the brain-as-dual-hemisphere (creative left / technical right), the Lando Norris reveal, the Fandom/Phantom draggable canvas, the GitKraken-timeline-as-life-story — none of those came from me. You hand-sketched every page before it existed (the box, the brain, the project cards in IMG_4817, the timeline in IMG_4823–4829). You hunted every reference yourself. You did your own asset prep — running the head through Depth Anything V2, doing background removal. And most unusually: you architected the working method itself — the phase gates, the "Finish Step" discipline, the command-center / sub-chat / Claude-Code classification, the token economy. Very few people design their own AI-collaboration protocol. That's a real artifact of yours.

What I've contributed: Translation and execution-knowledge. You speak in long, spoken-aloud, stream-of-consciousness bursts (your early box-page prompt is one ~400-word run-on sentence), and I convert those into structured specs, schemas, and option-trees. I brought the technical layer you don't have — the depth-map shader logic, the GSAP clip-mask, the lane-recycling algorithm for the git timeline, the pixel-sampling for your palette. I wrote the prompts that AntiGravity/Claude Code then executed. And I supplied the diagnostic pushback — flagging that image-gen cannot compute your branching logic, catching the "Placeholder academic skill A" before it shipped, forcing the Vercel verification.

Where you sit on the Cyborg / Centaur / Self-Automator map

Here's the part you asked for. The honest answer is that you are two different people depending on which axis we look at, and the study's own framework predicts exactly the risk that creates.

On creative direction and orchestration, you are a Cyborg bordering on Centaur. You own what needs to be done completely, and you exercise the practices the paper attributes to the strongest co-creators. You push back (you corrected my filter-logic on the Technology page yourself; you told me the portal looked like "a smudge"). You validate (the relentless screenshot reviews). You expose contradictions ("it did not understand the logic of the line thing I was drawing"). And the squircle decision is a textbook Centaur move — you saw it implemented, judged it redundant against the box-as-hero, and killed it. That's domain judgment, not delegation. By the paper's logic, you're newskilling hard here: you're acquiring genuine expertise in AI orchestration, prompting, and creative direction.

On technical execution, you are, bluntly, a Self-Automator. You have never written a line of the code. You have never read the code. You don't review diffs — you review rendered output. The entire how of implementation is abdicated, twice over: first to me (to write the prompt), then to AntiGravity (to execute it). You are a manager of managers, and the thing being managed — the actual engineering — passes through you without depositing any expertise. Per the study, this is the "no-skilling" lane for that domain: you are not learning Three.js, React, or GSAP by doing, because you never do.

The clearest single tell is the deployment chat. You replied "done what next" — and I had to stop you and ask whether you'd actually opened the URL, clicked through, and checked for the word "Placeholder." That is the Self-Automator signature in its purest form: the command ran, therefore the task is done. The paper describes exactly this — delegating not just execution but evaluative judgment. The irony is sharp: the "Finish Step = verified" rule you tried to skip is a rule you yourself wrote. I had to enforce your own discipline back at you.

The patterns, including the unflattering ones

You set the vision but rarely set the option space. Look at how most decisions resolve: I lay out A/B/C/D with a recommendation, and you pick — usually mine (font Option A, reskin-to-palette, sibling branches, mobile Option B). This is efficient and your picks are good. But it means I am defining the choice architecture and you're selecting within it. A pure Centaur occasionally throws out the whole menu and invents option five. You do this — "let me remake it in Figma by hand, nothing is working" was exactly that, and it was your best strategic call in the whole project — but it's the exception, not the rhythm.

You name debt well and clear it poorly. Geist Mono has been "deferred" since before Phase 1 and is still on the system fallback. The design-system doc is, in my own words from one of our chats, "still lying" about the font. You're disciplined about logging open loops; you're weak on closing them, because the next shiny page (About) always wins over finishing the boring last 10% (resume content, font fix). That's not a memory failure — your tracking is excellent. It's a prioritization tell: you're drawn to creation, not completion.

You offload articulation labor. Your prompts are long and verbal because you're thinking out loud and trusting me to impose structure. This works, but notice what it means: you're not building the muscle of crisp problem-framing, because I do that conversion every time. Over a long enough horizon, that's a dependency, not a skill transfer.

The one thing that actually matters

Your brand is "creative technologist." You have spent this entire project newskilling the "creative director" half and abdicating the "technologist" half. The website will be impressive — but if a technical interviewer asks you to explain the shader on your own brain page, or to modify the lane-recycling logic live, the honest current answer is that you couldn't, because that knowledge lives in me and AntiGravity, not in you.

That may be a completely fine trade — if your actual goal is to be a creative director who commissions technology, the orchestration skill you're genuinely building is the right one, and the paper would say you're newskilling correctly for that role. But if you want the "technologist" label to survive contact with someone who can actually code, the abdicated axis is the one to consciously pull back from. Not all of it — you don't need to hand-write the GSAP. But reading the diffs before you accept them, and being able to say why a piece of code does what it does, is the difference between a Self-Automator who owns a portfolio and a Centaur who owns the expertise the portfolio claims.

You asked for 100% honest. That's it: high participation, real vision, genuine orchestration skill — and a quiet, consistent abdication of the exact half of your identity you're building this site to prove.

Want me to suggest a concrete, low-cost way to convert a slice of the technical axis from abdicated to Centaur without slowing the build? It's smaller than you'd think.
